cycles.title: The Living Territories
cycles.description: The earliest represented civilizations organize life around watersheds, long-lived neighbors and the reach of a ruler’s road. Small settlements depend on particular living powers; larger states turn bodily gifts and old alliances into military authority.
cycles.sequenceNote: An opening reach of the represented past, not the origin of the world. The movement from local custodians to territorial states is a reconstruction across unmeasured time; their regions need not share one level of development.

eras.title: The long-lived margins
eras.description: At the edges of human settlement, custodians measure change through animals, seasons and the rise and disappearance of kingdoms.
context: Long-lived inhabitants maintain particular places and living populations.
Ecological routines and remembered local kingdoms establish deep histories without a mass urban infrastructure.
eras.sequenceNote: Their accumulated lifetimes belong to their own regions; neither story dates the first civilization.

eras.title: Villages of field and water
eras.description: Agrarian communities place healing, protection and seasonal work in the hands of a few specialists. A council, an orchard or a mill can carry as much practical weight as a distant ruler.
context: Farms, terraces, manual mills and harvests organize everyday work.
Mages, healers and guardians practice locally bounded powers through personal labor.
Councils and small communities negotiate the costs of medicine, defense and access.
eras.sequenceNote: The village histories are placed along one broad settlement era. Ninety years of barrier work, eleven flowering seasons and the held sunset retain their separate local clocks.

eras.title: The road and the march
eras.description: Territorial kingdoms extend beyond a single community. Armies, tribute and dynastic bargains carry power along roads and mountain passes, while refuges become political facts of their own.
context: Hereditary authority, military campaigns and negotiated alliances operate at a territorial scale.
Travel, provisions, hand weapons and siege work connect unevenly developed regions.
Embodied powers and nonhuman populations shape obligations inside states and across their borders.
eras.sequenceNote: This is a later territorial phase in the reconstruction. Each campaign and succession keeps its own dynasty and calendar; Ninepin’s short deployment stays entirely before extinction.

cycles.title: The Chartered Civilizations
cycles.description: Court patronage now shares authority with commercial roads, licensed trades and institutions that teach living power. The represented societies can sustain specialist careers beyond the ruler’s household, though inherited rank still shapes access.
cycles.sequenceNote: A broad succession after the territorial histories, with long gaps left open. Courts, road economies and colleges can coexist regionally; the chartered institutions are not asserted descendants of any earlier named state.

eras.title: Court and commoner
eras.description: Household power reaches into tenancy, service, luxury and inheritance. Magic can be a family expectation, a custom of protection or an object passed into someone else’s hands.
context: Noble households and unequal social standing govern ordinary obligations.
Personal magic and worked objects operate through craft, custom and inheritance.
Domestic spaces and patronage remain more prominent than mass technical services.
eras.sequenceNote: An established courtly society is the proposed context. The Second Wearing’s living inheritance is tentative here; the pendant’s maker and inaccessible storage interval remain undated.

eras.title: The hired road
eras.description: A road economy supports adventurers, smiths, clerics and other traveling specialists. Inn rooms, fairs and repair benches connect settlements without making them one kingdom.
context: Coaches, caravans, inns and public hiring create a commercial travel culture.
Specialist equipment and bounded magical services support livelihoods.
Reputations and printed notices circulate farther than individual households.
eras.sequenceNote: These journeys occupy the commercial reaches of the chartered period. Each curse and crossing has its own conditions; sanctuary travel does not date any other gate.

eras.title: The licensed arts
eras.description: Formal qualifications, source contracts and disciplined training turn unusual capacities into recognized work. Public works and colleges give practitioners a social place beyond heroic reputation.
context: Permits, examinations, contracts and teaching institutions regulate practice.
Living power requires technical skill, controlled material work or sustained bodily training.
Cities and professional communities support specialist careers and apprenticeships.
eras.sequenceNote: Kethra’s examination precedes her apprenticeship story directly, with an undated interval. The other institutions belong to this broader professional era without a claimed common founding.

eras.title: At Cinder Annex
eras.description: An infernal craft school admits living collaborators into an education organized around built work.
context: A formal school uses engineered craft, dispatch slates and assessed projects.
Constructed beings act as collaborators within an explicitly infernal social setting.
eras.sequenceNote: A contextual attachment to the age of formal practice. The Annex’s relation to the material world and its side of the extinction boundary are unresolved.

cycles.title: A Familiar World Dims
cycles.description: A later civilization combines familiar household technology with ordinary public magic, specialized schooling and a crowded sky. Farther along this reach, daily life has grown quieter: supermarkets and buses remain, while magic is treated as myth or encountered in private.
cycles.sequenceNote: The public modernity and later trough form a proposed local succession. Nell and Bash’s low-magic endpoint is established before the later gods and Glass Sea; the routes into Ravel keep their separate clocks.

eras.title: An ordinary extraordinary life
eras.description: Phones, laboratories and household appliances belong to a society in which magical property, unusual pupils and public transformations can be everyday concerns.
context: Familiar electronics, domestic appliances and laboratory work coexist with living magic.
Specialist schools and repair or property professions accommodate unusual capacities.
Public transformations and magical neighbors are familiar social facts.
eras.sequenceNote: This earlier public modernity precedes Northbridge in the reconstruction. Not About That’s pre-Bay reading position is supplied; no measured gap or school lineage is established.

eras.title: The quieter modernity
eras.description: Familiar streets and holiday homes continue, but the extraordinary is no longer the ordinary public framework. Exceptional encounters unfold through private routes, sleep and memory.
context: Supermarkets, buses and contemporary domestic life frame the material endpoint.
Magic is scarce, dismissed as myth or encountered through a private anomaly.
The material scenes coexist with crossings whose other coordinates are unsettled.
eras.sequenceNote: Nell and Bash’s material home belongs to the established old low-magic period. The later placement of the dream relay is editorial; its sixty-year separation and imprisonment are explicitly pre-extinction.

cycles.title: Gods and Civic Life
cycles.description: After the quieter modernity, later civilizations again organize public life around active powers. Divine offices govern grain and water; commercial regions work unfamiliar resources; eventually another familiar urban society supports schools, transit and public heroes.
cycles.sequenceNote: The emergence of later gods after the old low-magic trough is established. The succession from divine administrations to resource frontiers and civic hero modernity is editorial, allowing regional coexistence and further rises and falls.

eras.title: The offices of the gods
eras.description: Divinity has public duties: maintaining water, handling grain, serving a harbor or negotiating the practices of established faiths.
context: Gods or divine offices have visible roles in civic government and organized worship.
Water, grain and harbor work give religious power material responsibilities.
Mature records, offices and ritual obligations outlast individual disputes.
eras.sequenceNote: The two dragon governments share a plausible civic context but remain distinct states. Their two-century histories stay local; the shipwright’s office lasts fifty-seven minutes.

eras.title: The Salt Crucible
eras.description: An established religious order faces the bodily and social costs of opposed callings.
context: Religious vows and publicly recognized supernatural roles structure the conflict.
The crisis acts through living people and a local source of power.
eras.sequenceNote: Placed beside the period of public religious institutions. This local crisis is not identified with the later universal extinction.

eras.title: The worked frontiers
eras.description: Trading cities, mines and surveyed routes draw livelihoods from difficult environments. Instruments and repeated observation help people work around living powers and effects they cannot fully explain.
context: Mines, refineries, paid services and trade routes sustain specialist work.
Maps, hand tools, ledgers and material observation guide practical decisions.
Local ecologies or inherited workings can support livelihoods while remaining incompletely understood.
eras.sequenceNote: These resource economies form a proposed later reach. The Night Harvest convergence, buried fire and memory-bearing water retain unresolved mechanisms; none is classified as material-zero technology.

eras.title: Cities beneath public powers
eras.description: A renewed familiar modernity has schools, transit and communication networks alongside public heroism. Civic recovery and personal privacy must work in the same streets as extraordinary force.
context: Modern communication, schools and transit organize urban daily life.
Public heroes, villains or magical girls have recognizable social roles.
Communities face the practical aftermath of power: damaged services, privacy and mutual aid.
eras.sequenceNote: Brackenport’s nine years remain one local history. Northbridge’s showcase leads to the third-afternoon continuation and months of network growth; this whole era is placed before the Bay.

cycles.title: The Bay and Its Centuries
cycles.description: The Battle of the Bay breaks a public magical world. Its immediate aftermath struggles to identify the living; centuries later, a museum turns the disaster into a story its surviving witness can still correct.
cycles.sequenceNote: A directly connected local sequence occupies this turn without unrelated additions. Its centuries are not successive galactic orbits. The battle precedes the Glass Sea; the museum’s pre-extinction side remains editorial.

eras.title: Battle, aftermath, remembrance
eras.description: One crisis moves from a living battle to damaged civic records and then to an established museum culture.
context: The same Battle of the Bay anchors the event and its subsequent public record.
Damaged identification procedures precede institutional remembrance.
Solstice herself supplies the explicit centuries-later link to the museum.
eras.sequenceNote: Solstice → Dress → Count follows the supplied reading sequence. Dress’s prisoner is a different woman; the museum witness is Solstice. The exact interval to Dress is unestablished.

cycles.title: The Last Old Landscapes
cycles.description: Much later, whole populations depend on governed magical landscapes: flood prediction, protective districts and solar infrastructure. Still later inhabitants navigate structures whose builders and workings have faded from knowledge, before the final accounting ends every old material power.
cycles.sequenceNote: The Glass Sea is established after the earlier modernities and Bay. The surrounding civilizations and inhabited remnants form a proposed late succession, with no common collapse or builder imposed on them. All Accounts Due closes the old history.

eras.title: The governed landscape
eras.description: Cities and regional states distribute survival through living magical infrastructure. Public authorities decide who benefits from prediction, protection and stored responsibility.
context: Large populations depend on civic networks maintained through active living powers.
Government, records and technical specialists organize the distribution of risk.
Flood management, district protection and solar infrastructure operate at a landscape scale.
eras.sequenceNote: A later reconstruction of system-dependent civilizations. Sablewake’s local centuries and the Glass Sea’s four hundred years remain distinct; no shared energy system is inferred.

eras.title: The structures become the ground
eras.description: People travel through or build lives upon immense older structures. Survey, inherited records and practical procedure become the means of survival when origins no longer supply reliable explanations.
context: Older built environments have become inhabited or traversed geography.
Measurements, procedures and inherited knowledge guide present-day survival.
The structures’ makers and underlying mechanisms remain incompletely known.
eras.sequenceNote: These living frames are tentatively placed in late old history. The labyrinth’s construction and the colossus’s origin remain undated; a thousand years of hand-settlement ledgers is a local span.

eras.title: The final accounting
eras.description: The accumulating old systems reach the fixed event that ends them all.
context: The six old roots are explicitly identified and terminate together.
The Array’s construction and Faris’s accumulation supply local durations before the universal boundary.
eras.sequenceNote: Fixed extinction anchor: old material magic ends here, followed by perfect zero.

cycles.title: The Weight of Human Hands
cycles.description: The world continues through perfect material zero. A reactor city remembers magic as long dead; guilds, workshops and traveling communities build lives from machinery, ordinary organisms and bodily capacities. Industrial and road-bound regions need not prosper together.
cycles.sequenceNote: The first represented reach of the Long Dark is not its first generation. The order reconstructs a move from civic machinery toward more dispersed territorial power as civilizations’ fortunes vary.

eras.title: The civic machine
eras.description: Public infrastructure and small workshops depend on maintained physical devices. Practical knowledge matters from the reactor system to the repair bench and the handling of a common organism.
context: Machinery, maintenance and measured physical behavior support ordinary work.
Guilds, workshops and public infrastructure distribute technical expertise.
Cities and smaller communities have unequal engineering capacities.
eras.sequenceNote: A material engineering context after magic has died. Orison’s fall has no established causal relation to these other settlements.

eras.title: The road polities
eras.description: States and communities hold together through travel, trade and embodied labor. Diverse populations negotiate political borders and intimate obligations without requiring operative enchantment.
context: Territorial rulers, caravans and physical travel connect local societies.
Bodily capacities and nonhuman biology shape work and household life.
Political authority remains local enough for refuge, marriage and bargaining to alter its course.
eras.sequenceNote: A later territorial reach in the reconstruction. Different populations can share material history without belonging to one court or lineage.

cycles.title: Crowns and Chartered Streets
cycles.description: A later set of civilizations concentrates authority in palaces and armies while towns sustain professional, mercantile and domestic institutions. Material history again has courts, but their rulers inherit no functioning old magic.
cycles.sequenceNote: A proposed later consolidation of territorial and urban life. Imperial centers and chartered towns represent regional forms of authority, not a single empire extending across every story.

eras.title: The imperial household
eras.description: Palace decisions extend into armies, capitals and family life. Household relationships become matters of public power, while practical rescue still comes down to tools and labor.
context: Rulers, capitals and standing military forces give households public reach.
Marriage, inheritance and returning relatives affect territorial authority.
Physical travel, weapons and manual work dominate the represented action.
eras.sequenceNote: The capital’s seventeen-year absence and each family episode remain local. Save That Dragon’s placement is tentative: the rescue uses ropes and winches, while the dragon’s fire is unclassified.

eras.title: The chartered street
eras.description: Urban associations and settled customs shape work, courtship and care. Rank remains visible, but professional services and civic markets give people other ways to organize a life.
context: Established professions, associations and hired care support urban households.
Markets, social conventions and public reputations shape everyday dealings.
Long-lived residents and ordinary bodily needs coexist within material society.
eras.sequenceNote: These towns occupy the wider civic period. The elf caregiver’s almost two centuries and eighteen years with the twins stay within her own household history.

cycles.title: A Familiar Meridian
cycles.description: Another long reach arrives at recognizably modern streets: festivals, cafés, phones and ordinary private lives. Elsewhere in this broad period, mature engineering lets dynastic and private ambitions reach into genetic history and orbit.
cycles.sequenceNote: The familiar present is a small region of an immense material history. The reconstructed pharaohs’ roughly ten-thousand-year gap stays within this broad cycle rather than implying galactic orbits between ancient genetic sources and their arrival.

eras.title: The familiar street
eras.description: Modern services and institutions support lives whose decisive events can fit inside a conversation, a season or a family home.
context: Familiar modern technology and everyday urban or domestic institutions frame the living scenes.
Relationships, employment and bodily life require no operative material magic.
Immediate local calendars matter more to the characters than deep planetary history.
eras.sequenceNote: The proposed familiar-present interval includes Ruth’s material life only. Her station belongs to an unresolved afterlife coordinate, not an exception to zero.

eras.title: Engineered sovereignty
eras.description: Private wealth and dynastic claims operate through mature material engineering. Reconstructed ancestry and orbital leverage put extraordinary tools inside recognizable political negotiations.
context: Advanced biological or orbital engineering is available to political actors.
Households and private interests make claims that reach beyond domestic life.
Contemporary legal and commercial arrangements regulate the resulting disputes.
eras.sequenceNote: A technologically mature reach of the same broad meridian. Genetic reconstruction is not continuous life or memory; the tea party is not assigned to another story’s orbital program.

cycles.title: The Manufactured Citizen
cycles.description: Later technical civilizations make bodies, identity and perception into services—and into assets institutions can own or command. Domestic repair grows beside consumer reconstruction, controlled cities and military systems, with different regions drawing the boundary of personhood differently.
cycles.sequenceNote: A proposed expansion of material capabilities after the familiar meridian. The progression concerns social reach, from household technology to civic and military command; it does not establish one technological lineage or one war.

eras.title: Modified neighbourhoods
eras.description: Bionics and synthetic bodies enter ordinary neighborhoods. Repairs, services and hallway encounters show how advanced manufacture becomes part of domestic life.
context: Bionic or synthetic bodies are present in domestic and neighborhood settings.
Repair work, private services and ordinary urban institutions support daily life.
Personhood is negotiated through familiar social encounters as well as technical care.
eras.sequenceNote: An everyday phase of manufactured embodiment, with separate households and service economies.

eras.title: Bodies on demand
eras.description: Commercial and medical systems can revise appearance, rebuild combatants or restore a recorded neural state. The material consequences outside the body remain.
context: Genetic modification, bodily reconstruction or neural intervention is technically developed.
Medical and commercial institutions mediate access to altered bodies and identities.
The changes remain physical processes with limits and continuing external consequences.
eras.sequenceNote: These capabilities occupy a broader consumer and institutional period. The one-charge neural restoration does not rewind the outside world.

eras.title: The city that accounts for you
eras.description: Data systems decide who can move, be recognized or possess a history. Urban infrastructure becomes an instrument of corporate and civic authority.
context: Ubiquitous networks, surveillance and automated urban services govern daily movement.
Institutions claim authority through registration, visibility or control of records.
Excluded people and censored histories expose the limits of apparently complete civic knowledge.
eras.sequenceNote: A proposed period of pervasive urban control. Each city has its own present and concealed past; the stories do not establish one administration.

eras.title: Commanded lives
eras.description: Military and civic systems treat bodies and experience as deployable assets. Operators confront the difference between executing a command and retaining a life.
context: Engineered command systems control combat, defense or deployable bodies.
Institutional programming can outlast peace, service or the wishes of the person inside it.
Human decisions and bodily limits remain consequential within advanced machinery.
eras.sequenceNote: The local peace-to-war sequence, four years in Unit 02 and thirty-year Jovian watch remain separate histories. Their position implies no common enemy or shared campaign.

cycles.title: The Inhabited Ruins
cycles.description: What technical civilizations leave behind becomes the setting for new lives. Some communities salvage or misunderstand older works; others build mature ecological cities whose varied districts and migrating traditions belong to the same present.
cycles.sequenceNote: A recovery and rebuilding reach after histories have been lost. Technological inequality remains geographic as well as temporal: a ruined frontier and an illuminated city can be contemporaries.

eras.title: The buried territories
eras.description: Descendants, salvagers and scouts read material remains with incomplete inherited knowledge. Their discoveries reveal how unevenly a civilization’s past can survive.
context: Lost technical histories persist through sealed works, ruins and salvage.
Present communities recover or interpret remnants through practical exploration.
Neighboring regions can retain very different levels of technology and historical knowledge.
eras.sequenceNote: Each loss has its own history. The room’s two local stages stay together; the scouts’ five centuries after war do not date the neighboring city to an earlier universal age.

eras.title: The living city
eras.description: Rebuilding uses ecology, climate and collective resources as infrastructure. Mature technical systems coexist with local building traditions and inherited routes.
context: Material or biological engineering supports housing, water and environmental management.
Cities and communities negotiate common resources through everyday institutions.
Long-standing local forms and advanced technology can share a present.
eras.sequenceNote: A renewed civic reach of material history. Living tissue, condensation and accumulated architecture do not require surviving old magic.

cycles.title: The World Beneath Its Sky
cycles.description: The material world expands again into the inheritance above it. Surface communities and old orbital structures have kept different histories; farther along, stellar roads make humanity itself an ancient presence to be encountered and interpreted.
cycles.sequenceNote: A late represented expansion through inherited orbital and stellar infrastructure. Earlier builders and departures remain undated, and no common exodus is imposed. Reawakening lies beyond this whole material reach.

eras.title: Divided sky and ground
eras.description: Long-lived orbital works survive beside surface populations whose knowledge of them has changed. Contact exposes gaps between inhabited history and official explanation.
context: Orbital stations or large space structures have long local histories.
Surface and space communities preserve different knowledge of the same physical environment.
Communication and observation reveal inherited infrastructure that has been misread or forgotten.
eras.sequenceNote: Eight centuries of teaching belong to the kite correspondence alone. The stations, sunshade and migrations are not assigned common builders.

eras.title: The old stellar roads
eras.description: Old spacefaring infrastructure meets grounded life, and people encounter humanity as something already carried through a very long history.
context: Ancient spacefaring works or routes remain materially consequential.
Present travelers and grounded communities interpret inherited human traces.
Technical observation connects local lives to histories beyond the surface.
eras.sequenceNote: The living frames occupy the far represented Long Dark. Their earlier stellar histories keep open coordinates; ordinary light can still cross the ages toward the fixed return.

cycles.title: The World Learns New Workings
cycles.description: The first reciprocal working ends perfect zero. Much later societies build common crafts, living rites and hereditary institutions around active powers; a further industrial reach develops professions around the body’s own channels.
cycles.sequenceNote: The return is fixed; the later civilizations are placed after an unmeasured development interval. New workings do not restore the six old roots. Rural, courtly and industrial forms occupy different reaches of one renewed planetary history.

eras.title: The first link
eras.description: Ordinary light reaches a living encounter and the first reciprocal working begins.
context: The established chronology ends perfect zero at this encounter.
The new working depends on a living reciprocal relation and does not restore an old system.
eras.sequenceNote: Fixed reawakening anchor. The earlier fall belongs to the extinction endpoint; its carried light crosses the Long Dark.

eras.title: The common workings
eras.description: Local craft and rural life have learned to deal with active living power. Names, timber and everyday livelihoods carry obligations that must be worked out in person.
context: Small communities and local trades organize daily life.
Living magical effects act through practical relationships rather than mass technical systems.
Craft work and reciprocity determine what a person can safely ask of a working.
eras.sequenceNote: A mature local era after the first link, with enough time for inherited buildings and established practices. The Hollow Cask’s twelve-week plan stays local.

eras.title: The ritual kingdoms
eras.description: Hereditary states recognize living rites, magical professions and unusual creatures as political facts. Regional communities must negotiate those powers in succession, public service and war.
context: Hereditary governments and settled regional communities structure public authority.
Active living rites, creature capacities and magical professionals affect civic decisions.
Long local records and practical travel or siege work coexist with supernatural power.
eras.sequenceNote: These kingdoms follow the common-working reach in the reconstruction. Forecasting’s three centuries, suspended injury and Shalegate’s three-night siege remain separate local spans.

eras.title: The marked lives
eras.description: An industrial society organizes craft and clinical intervention around the marks everyone is born carrying.
context: Dye works, inspection lamps and clinical professions support a developed craft economy.
A universal birthmark convention shapes family expectations and access to bodily faculties.
eras.sequenceNote: A distinct later bodily regime. Its birth-channel rule is not merged with the much later proposed society of eighteenth-year transformations.

cycles.title: The Powers Beneath the Streets
cycles.description: Later craft societies confront divine claims and unfamiliar machinery. A renewed modernity then lays vehicles, electric services and domestic routines over older obligations, household agents and routes that still work.
cycles.sequenceNote: The reconstruction crosses another long change in civic life, from hand-worked technical communities to familiar streets with accumulated supernatural histories. Local powers retain distinct conditions and origins.

eras.title: Craft before divine claims
eras.description: Skilled workers bring practical knowledge to encounters with apparent or actual divinity. Bodies, tools and civic damage put limits on what higher status can accomplish.
context: Experienced manual specialists use bodily knowledge and practical tools.
Inhabited settlements and built works bear the consequences of unusual powers.
The action depends on bounded material or living conditions, even when a participant claims divine authority.
eras.sequenceNote: A shared craft context for two distinct encounters. The regenerating claimant and the god of death are not assigned one species, theology or mechanism.

eras.title: The mill room
eras.description: A working mill town encounters a growing machine whose apparent observers claim a higher perspective.
context: Mill repair, couriers, ledgers and physical routes organize the settlement.
Residents use experiments and practical engineering to investigate an intrusive mechanism.
eras.sequenceNote: Tentatively attached to the same broad technical reach. The machine’s ontology and the players’ external coordinate remain unresolved.

eras.title: Old agreements under new roads
eras.description: Modern towns carry obligations their redevelopment cannot simply erase. A public road, a building site or a bus journey meets a still-operative local history.
context: Vehicles, electric services or civic development frame the present.
Place-bound obligations and routes remain active beneath familiar infrastructure.
Generations of local history affect movement, property and public responsibility.
eras.sequenceNote: A later modern reach with accumulated local pasts. The promise, threshold and bus route retain different mechanisms and destinations.

eras.title: Household inheritances
eras.description: Inherited companions, family instruments and old divine relations enter modern domestic routines. The household becomes a meeting place between a familiar present and durable personal obligations.
context: Contemporary domestic life frames the active supernatural relationship.
Families inherit agents, objects or relationships with histories older than the immediate event.
Access and consequences are personal and household-bound rather than a public hero profession.
eras.sequenceNote: The mature domestic reaches of this modernity. The Fenwick activations, audit Tuesdays and later overwrite stay in one local family sequence.

cycles.title: Lives Between Ordinary and Uncanny
cycles.description: A later familiar society accommodates the extraordinary mainly through private lives, mixed households and negotiated crossings. Schools, phones and everyday services persist, while families decide what can be shared and institutions regulate particular thresholds.
cycles.sequenceNote: A long domestic and civic reach after the inherited-obligation societies. Regional conventions vary; private powers need not have the same visibility everywhere, and no universal transformation rule is inferred.

eras.title: The private powers
eras.description: Ordinary work, school and home life frame powers whose consequences are intimate and bounded. Most of the surrounding social world carries on without a public heroic role for the person involved.
context: Familiar phones, schooling, work or domestic routines frame the living scene.
Anomalies act through a particular person, object or encounter.
Identity, memory and privacy are handled outside a professional hero institution.
eras.sequenceNote: The living frames share this proposed private-power era. Four dawns and thirteen years remain local; the road trip’s altered routes and reversals keep unsettled clocks.

eras.title: The mixed household
eras.description: Human and nonhuman relatives share recognizable family routines. Daily services, bodily limits and cultural privacy matter as much as extraordinary identity.
context: Modern homes and everyday services support family or intimate relationships.
Human and nonhuman lives coexist within domestic social arrangements.
Care, bodily difference and cultural privacy require negotiated everyday practices.
eras.sequenceNote: An extended household era with regional differences. Each family retains its own biology, practice and history; the wolf rescue and later visit remain a short local sequence.

eras.title: The negotiated crossing
eras.description: Contemporary human institutions encounter regulated passages into supernatural polities and markets. The journey brings conditions that continue after someone comes home.
context: Phones, hospitals or higher education establish a modern human endpoint.
Crossings involve organized supernatural polities or regulated transactions.
Local rules and limited access constrain travel and its consequences.
eras.sequenceNote: Only the human material frames are placed here. Deepmarket and the infernal realm retain their own unresolved coordinates and rules.

cycles.title: Power Enters Public Life
cycles.description: Another modern reach makes unusual capacities into public professions and civic problems. Training and response systems develop beside ordinary accommodations; elsewhere media turns predictive power into coercion, and a later bodily regime reorganizes coming of age.
cycles.sequenceNote: A proposed shift toward publicly organized power after the private and household reach. Professional heroes, ordinary urban users and a coercive broadcast city represent regional differences; the universal eighteenth-year convention belongs to a distinct later era.

eras.title: The public profession
eras.description: Colleges, patrols and established hero or villain identities make extraordinary power a recognizable occupation. Friendship and family life must fit around that public role.
context: Public hero, villain or magical-girl roles have established social recognition.
Training, patrol, response or medical support organizes the use of power.
Professional identities reach into family, college and domestic life.
eras.sequenceNote: A mature public-power era after the household reach. Its institutions are not continuations of Northbridge or the Bay across extinction.

eras.title: Power in the ordinary city
eras.description: Urban lives accommodate unusual personal capacities through equipment, habits and practical limits. The consequences appear in rooms, journeys and daily relationships.
context: Familiar urban infrastructure and domestic routines frame active personal powers.
Equipment, rules or bodily costs constrain how those powers can be used.
Practical accommodation matters beyond a professional hero identity.
eras.sequenceNote: A civic companion to the professional era. Shrinking, sleep travel and lightning transit retain separate limits and do not constitute one transport network.

eras.title: The coercive airwaves
eras.description: A modern industrial city lives under a predictive broadcast that turns private suffering into public leverage.
context: Radio, garages, freight work and emergency services establish a mature urban economy.
An involuntary supernatural broadcast supports blackmail and civic fear.
eras.sequenceNote: A distinct regional regime within the public-power reach. Its changing predictions and blood-linked practice are local, not the same process as the Fenwick watch.

eras.title: The eighteenth-year world
eras.description: A later society has built family expectations and institutional recognition around a universal change at eighteen.
context: A universal maturation event structures the passage into adult identity.
Established households and institutions recognize and manage the resulting forms.
eras.sequenceNote: A distinct later bodily era. The eighteenth-year convention is not combined with the earlier birthmark society into an invented universal rule.

cycles.title: The World Remembers Imperfectly
cycles.description: Later societies inherit more past than they can reliably explain. Excavators, expedition specialists, museum agents and a therapist examine places, objects and living memories; another traveler returns to a familiar home from destinations that will not fit one calendar.
cycles.sequenceNote: The farthest represented modern frames gather around mature practices of investigation and return. Deep departures, ancient battles, object makers and other destinations remain open rather than being assigned invented extinction crossings.

eras.title: The examined past
eras.description: Specialists investigate inherited or unearthed evidence with developed methods and limited access. Old places, objects and memories resist easy identification with the histories people expected.
context: Excavation, expedition work, museum practice or therapy provides specialist methods of inquiry.
An inherited object, place or living history is materially present in a later social world.
Observation establishes bounded evidence while deeper causes or dates can remain unresolved.
eras.sequenceNote: Only the excavation arrival, expedition, house visit and therapy frames are placed here. The displaced village’s departure and the ancient battle retain separately unresolved coordinates.

eras.title: The returned traveler
eras.description: A familiar apartment becomes the home endpoint of a life spent moving among assignments with other clocks.
context: A contemporary apartment supplies a recognizable living home frame.
An organized assignment sequence connects that frame to multiple destinations.
eras.sequenceNote: The homecoming is placed beside this later modernity. All ten assignments and their destinations remain separately undated.

where-the-white-elk-went.note: The guardian remembers kingdoms through a continuing relationship with one living boundary. Its long ecological custody suits the earliest represented margins without dating the world’s beginning.

the-last-flames.note: The keeper’s long memory and the dragons’ arrival belong to a living refuge beyond ordinary state administration. The unnamed threat remains unresolved.

the-villages-only-mage.note: The village’s dependence on one practitioner sits within a wider culture of traveling mages. Local need, rather than a formal public network, organizes access to power.

the-ninety-year-barrier.note: Ninety years of the witch’s work precede the child’s breach. A small community depends on sustained personal protection across that whole local interval.

every-flower-she-knew.note: Eleven flowering seasons precede one storm-bound harvest. Local plant knowledge and bounded medicine support this agrarian placement; the effect’s underlying category remains unsettled.

blood-types-of-immortality.note: Nine years of blood research proceed through weather instruments, living samples and negotiated access. The work is a local practitioner’s history, not the origin of later healing institutions.

tea-for-the-first-guest.note: A roadside tower and passing carts connect a roughly two-thousand-year-old wizard to the local settled landscape. His centuries of waiting remain inside this living frame.

the-unfinished-sunset.note: The ronin returns after twenty years to a village held within its sunset. Agricultural life inside and elapsed time outside retain different experiences of that local interval.

connections.note: The prose identifies its living museum witness as Solstice Evening Bell, centuries after the same Battle of the Bay. Battle and museum remain in one close local arc; the museum’s pre-extinction side remains editorial.

connections.label: The archmage becomes a teacher
connections.note: Voice establishes Kethra’s qualification; Lock begins with the same named archmage taking a mistreated apprentice and uses her call-link practice. The interval is not dated.

connections.label: Two arrangements for twelve dragons
connections.note: Kharost’s rotating Crown offices and Varkesh’s collective Sleepless Majesty share a civic context of resources, records and divine government. They make different bargains with sleep and remain distinct states, not a shared cast or sequel.

connections.label: A home is also a living body
connections.note: Agnes exposes coerced structural labor; Lirenn discovers occupied volume inside living leased rooms. The echo connects a renewed-magical craft society and a much earlier material city without asserting shared biology or building lineage.

connections.label: Who can claim a memory?
connections.note: One-use sensory fragments from retrieved objects and licensed neural extraction make distinct memory problems. The resemblance is thematic, not a shared substance or technological ancestry.

connections.label: The record beneath the monument
connections.note: A museum’s heroic reconstruction and a drowned-king interpretation meet more limited evidence. This is a reader parallel about misremembered history, not a common archive.

connections.label: Humanity becomes an inheritance
connections.note: A dinosaur surface polity and a later stellar courier encounter different human legacies. No common departure, station network, or absolute order is established.

connections.label: Learning what the creatures actually do
connections.note: Route observations change how people respond to shadow beasts and throat-node-bearing creatures. The stories establish no common species, invasion, or mechanism.

connections.label: A useful organism changes the question
connections.note: Both communities must reconsider handling practices after observing effects. The slime’s material behavior does not classify the Night Harvest effect or date either settlement.

connections.label: When the ground stops being a promise
connections.note: Evacuation requires precise counts when an inhabited hand moves and when Orison loses lift. The colossus is not assigned a reactor cause; these are not the same fall.

connections.label: The past arrives in a new present
connections.note: An intact displaced village and genetically reconstructed adults confront later institutions. Actual temporal transport and reconstruction remain different processes, not one refounding event.

connections.label: A person falls outside the map
connections.note: A threshold working disrupts a public road; a networked city cannot place an unregistered passenger. The people, technologies, and causes differ, despite the shared recognition problem.

connections.label: The destination keeps its own clock
connections.note: An assignment sequence and the Ravel encounter both resist a flat timeline. Their resemblance proves neither one portal network nor that Ryo’s destinations are Ravel.

connections.label: Crossings bring obligations home
connections.note: Bearer-powered sanctuary crossings and a living market seam both impose local limits. No mechanism, underworld, or ancient route is shared by implication.

connections.label: Company at a threshold
connections.note: Borrowed living hosts and a stranded afterlife traveler create different obligations to another person. The parallel establishes no common possession or station mechanism.

connections.label: A political offer needs a person’s answer
connections.note: Royal negotiation meets the independent will of the people inside it. This is an ethical parallel between unrelated courts, not a dynasty or a continuation of Ninepin.

connections.label: What the inherited promise costs
connections.note: A solar polity and a witch’s town confront responsibilities accumulated over generations. The juxtaposition does not make promise-binding a descendant of solar fire.

connections.label: A name that can be chosen
connections.note: Different pressures around names and identity invite a joint reading. The stories do not share a name-magic rule, heroic lineage, or cast.

connections.label: One family, unequal capacities
connections.note: An elf caregiver and the mortal eldest of a divine household experience family obligations with unequal capacities. The material town and much later magical household retain different lifespans, practices and histories.
